afford.adjustHint: Change anything below to see how the ceiling moves.
afford.bindingCash: Your down payment is the limit
afford.bindingCashFlow: Your monthly budget is the limit
afford.bindingCashFlowHint: Saving more will not raise this number — the mortgage has to fit your monthly income. A raise, or lower fixed spending, is what moves it.
afford.bindingCashHint: Keeping a safety buffer after buying is what caps this. Every bit you save lifts it — and by more than you save.
afford.bindingLiquid: Cash on hand is the limit
afford.bindingLiquidHint: You have the income for a larger loan, but not yet the cash for the down payment. This one is pure time and saving.
afford.disclaimer: Assumes a safety buffer of six months of your own expenses after buying, and that you keep at least a tenth of your income spare each month. Projections hold your spending flat and are an estimate, not advice.
afford.leverage: Every {{saved}} you put aside raises what you can afford by about {{unlocked}} — a down payment is leverage.
afford.limitLiquid: Cash you can actually hand over
afford.noSurplus: Your spending currently matches or exceeds your income, so this ceiling will not rise on its own. Freeing up even a small monthly amount starts moving it — and thanks to the down-payment leverage above, it moves faster than you might expect.
afford.plateauNote: This levels off because your income — not your savings — becomes the limit. Tick the box above to see what steady raises would do.
afford.returnHint: Affects the projection only — today’s ceiling uses what you already hold.
afford.subtitleAdjusted: Showing an adjusted scenario — not your live figures.
afford.subtitleNoData: Add a few months of transactions to base this on your real habits.
afford.subtitleReal: From your own income and spending ({{basis}}-mo average) — not a guess.
afford.title: What can you afford right now?
afford.noIncomeHint: There's no recorded income in your last 12 complete months, so a price would just read NT$0. Record your income, or enter a monthly income below, to see what you can afford.

glide.crossedAlready: You are no longer a net borrower
glide.crossover: Leverage reaches 1× in ~{{y}} years, at age {{age}}
glide.crossoverHint: That is the milestone worth tracking — it moves when you save more, and barely moves when the market has a good quarter.
glide.debtFree: Loans fully repaid in {{y}} years (age {{age}}) · {{interest}} interest still ahead
glide.discountHint: A modest real rate — not the equity return. Higher discounting shrinks the target.
glide.maxLevHint: Never above 2:1 — the book is explicit about this.
glide.noCrossoverHint: At these savings the debt never stops outweighing your own money. Raise savings or lower the target share.
glide.note: A projection, not a forecast: it assumes a steady return and that you keep saving. Loan repayments already sit in your recorded expenses, so the payment is added back to savings the month the loan clears.
glide.share: Target share of lifetime wealth in stocks
glide.shareHint: The book's own default is 83%; most people who run this for real sit between 50% and 67%.
glide.subtitle: Target leverage falls on its own as savings accumulate. Your job is to follow it down, not to predict the market.
glide.title: The glidepath

history.title: Leverage over time
history.subtitle: Today’s ratio cannot tell you whether you are deleveraging. The direction can.
history.overCeiling: {{n}} days above your {{max}}× ceiling in this window.
history.equityShare: No investment debt in this window, so the line is your equity share rather than leverage: the portion of your net assets held as stock. It only becomes leverage above 1×.
history.downByRepaying: Leverage fell and so did the debt — this is the strategy working, not the market flattering it.
history.downByMarket: Leverage fell while the debt stayed put, so the portfolio rose. Real progress, but it can reverse without you doing anything.
history.upDespiteRepaying: Leverage rose even though you repaid — the portfolio fell faster than the loan did.
history.upByBorrowing: Leverage rose on flat or growing debt. Check that this was a decision rather than a drift.
history.flat: Leverage held steady across this window.
history.underwater: {{n}} days with no ratio to report: investment debt exceeded everything you owned, and the line breaks across them.
history.empty: No balance history for this window yet. It is replayed from your recorded transactions and holdings, so it fills in as those accumulate.
history.basis: Both halves are measured, not projected: balances are replayed from your transactions and holdings, and past debt from the payments recorded against each loan — the same payments that set the balance shown today.

loans.addOne: Add one on the Loans page
loans.autoSelected: Your personal loans are counted as investment debt by default. Untick any that funded something else.
loans.hint: Only these count as investment debt. A mortgage or car loan affects net worth but is not part of the strategy.
loans.title: Which loans funded the portfolio?

lifecycle.pageSubtitle: Borrowing young spreads your market exposure across more years. Track the leverage, the spread, and the date you stop being a borrower.

phase.accumulateHint: Your future savings still dwarf your portfolio, so the target exposure is capped by the leverage ceiling rather than by your own money.
phase.deleverageHint: Savings have grown enough that the target leverage now falls every year on its own. No market call required.
phase.glideHint: Leverage is done. From here the strategy gradually lowers your equity share as retirement approaches.
phase.underwaterHint: Investment debt exceeds everything you own. Reduce the debt before adding any exposure.

position.gapBreach: Leverage is above the {{max}}× ceiling. Reduce debt or exposure before anything else on this page matters.
position.gapOver: {{amount}} above target — let savings catch up rather than adding more.
position.gapUnder: Room for {{amount}} more exposure before you hit the target.
position.title: Leverage today

principles.subtitle: Leverage is only defensible with guardrails. These are the ones that keep a bad market from becoming a permanent loss.
principles.title: Rules of the strategy

home.shortfallSub: more than your cash and investments together
home.title: If you bought a home
home.none: Save a buy-vs-rent scenario on the house plan page (in this browser) to see what the purchase does to your leverage.
home.subtitle: {{name}}: {{amount}} leaves at closing, from Life cash then investments; the Emergency fund stays a reserve. The house is not a financial asset, so net financial assets fall by all of it.
home.monthlySub: mortgage and upkeep, less the rent that stops

safety.sliderAmplified: At {{lev}}× a {{drop}}% fall costs you {{loss}}% of your own money — the loan does not fall with the market.
safety.sliderUnlevered: Unlevered, a fall costs your own money no more than the market fell.
safety.coverageBody: Free cash flow before the payment is {{surplus}}/mo. Aim for 2× or more.
safety.forcedSaleBody: Your free cash flow or your reserves are too thin to carry the payment through a rough patch. Fix this before adding exposure — it matters more than the leverage ratio.
safety.note: Drops apply to the stock exposure only; cash and reserves are assumed intact. Leverage rises after a fall because the debt does not shrink with the market.
safety.runwayBody: How long your reserves keep paying with zero income, without selling stock. Aim for 12 months.
safety.runwayNone: No payment to fund from reserves.
safety.subtitle: The loan payment is due whatever the market does. Being forced to sell holdings to make it is the one failure the strategy cannot recover from.
safety.title: Can you survive a bad market?
safety.wipeoutPost: takes your own money to zero. That is simply 1 ÷ leverage — the price of the ratio above.
safety.wipeoutSafe: With no net leverage, no market drop alone can wipe out your own money.
safety.wipeoutUnderwater: Your investment debt already exceeds everything you own, so every drawdown below leaves you underwater. Reduce the debt first.

spread.twrBasis: Time-weighted since {{since}}: your own deposits are taken out, so it measures the investments, not the saving.
spread.ifRunToTerm: if the loans run to term
spread.negative: The borrowed {{debt}} is currently costing about {{carry}} a year more than it earns. One bad stretch does not invalidate the strategy, but a persistent negative spread does.
spread.positive: The borrowed {{debt}} is earning about {{carry}} a year more than it costs. Expect this to swing hard year to year — the case for leverage rests on long-run averages, never on any single year.
spread.subtitle: Measured, not assumed: the rate your loans actually charge against the return your holdings actually delivered.
spread.title: Is the leverage paying for itself?
spread.unknown: No annualized return yet — holdings need enough history for an IRR before the spread means anything.
